question: The first violin ends Dvořáks "Symphony no. 2, Op. 4" on three notes. Which is the lowest one?

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The lowest of the three notes the first violins land on at the very close of the finale is E.

In the coda of the 4th movement the tutti is brought to a huge B♭ major close and the first violins are given the final three-note tag that punctuates the whole symphony. In the full score the figure is written out in a high position and then dropped for the tag, and the last descent is read in the part as A – G – E in the lower octave of the staff, the E sounding just below the staff in the first desk. That E is the bass note of the closing triplet; the semitone step G–E is what gives the final cadential pull into the tonic B♭ – D – F chord that the orchestra sustains under it, so in the actual sounding line of the first violins the lowest pitch they strike on the final three-note gesture is that E, after which the section holds the tonic triad.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the Allegro con fuoco finale the work is closed in its tonic
B♭ major.  The last gestural figure of the 1st violins is the tonic triad
of that key written as an ascending / closing arpeggio

      B♭ – D – F

in the 1st-violin staff, i.e. the root–third–fifth of the final B♭-major
tutti.  The three pitches are the same triad that the whole orchestra
holds in the final B♭-major chord.  In that three-note closing figure the
root is the lowest pitch, the final sounding tonic

    B♭

the B♭ that is the root of the closing B♭-major triad, normally printed
in the 1st violins as the B♭4–D5–F5 arpeggio, the B♭ being the lowest of
the three written pitches and the note on which the first-violin line
actually comes to rest.  This is the tonic of the symphony, B♭ major,
sounding in effect the tonic B♭ of the final chord.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The finale is in the tonic B♭ major and the first-violin part is
closed by the tonic arpeggio which is written in the last bars of the
Allegro con fuoco as the final B♭–major sonority.

In the usual performing edition the last three pitches that the 1st
violins actually sound are the three notes of the tonic triad in the
coda, normally written

  f′ – d′ – b♭

in descending order, i.e. in ascending order b♭ – d – f.  The
sonority is the B♭ major tonic B♭–D–F, and the note that is heard last
and which is the lowest of the three is the tonic

B♭

the B♭ that closes the movement, in the first-violin staff about b♭4,
the b♭ that is the bottom of the final B♭–D–F arpeggio.  It is the
tonic B♭ of the piece, the last pitch of the final B♭-major
arpeggiation, and therefore the lowest of the three closing notes.
In the printed part this is the B♭ below the top of the staff, the
final b♭ of the f–d–b♭ descent, i.e. the tonic B♭ of the symphony.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In the published full score the coda of the Finale is a straight
tonic affirmation in B♭ major. The first violins finish the work with the
broken tonic triad

B♭ – D – F

written in the upper register of the instrument, the three distinct
melodic pitches that are actually written out on the last bar of the
movement being the B♭ major arpeggio up to the tonic.  In the
ordinary modern edition that is the F of the triad that is the lowest
pitch the first-desk part actually articulates on the last three
attack-points of the movement, about F4 in the first-violin staff,
F5 in the sounding octave that is usually quoted, the B♭–D–F being the
tonic triad of B♭ major.  In pitch-class terms the triad is the B♭
major triad and the B♭ is the bass of the three-note tonic arpeggio,
the D and the F lying above it, so that the lowest pitch class of the
closing figure is B♭, the lowest written first-violin pitch of the
three-note figure being the F of the broken triad.

6.text:
In the coda of the last, Allegro con fuoco, movement the orchestra closes
on a B flat major tutti. In the printed parts the first violins close the
coda with the ordinary B flat-major arpeggiation which is written
descending in the last two bars of the movement

      F – D – B♭

in the violin's register, F5–D5–B♭4 in the ordinary modern edition, 
the B♭ being the bass of the arpeggio.  It is the tonic B♭ of the
symphony, the bottom note of the three-note closing arpeggiation which
is the bottom of the final B♭–D–F sonority, often quoted as the B♭
that underlies the last bar of the work.  That is the lowest pitch the
first desks touch on the way to the final fermata on B♭ major.

4.text:
The close of the 4th mvt. Vivace is a normal D major perfect authentic
cadence.  In the last coda the first violins get the D-major triad
in the melody

      D – F♯ – A

the three pitch classes of the tonic which are the last three
pitches that the desk actually plays before the tutti D-major
fermata is taken.  In the printed score that is the familiar
D–F♯–A arpeggiation of the final closing gesture, normally written
as D5–F♯5–A5 / D6–F♯6–A6 according to the edition, the bottom
member of the figure being the tonic

D.

The three–note figure is normally written in the violin as an
ascending / descending D-major arpeggio D–F♯–A, the D being the
lowest pitch class of the three-note close, the tonic of the
symphony, the D above middle C, D5 in the normal reading, the
D6 of the final arpeggiation in the full score.  That is the
F♯–A–D  /  D–F♯–A  triad that is the first-violin’s last sounding
material, so the bottom note of the three-note termination is the
tonic D, with F♯ and A a major third and a fifth above it.

12.text:
The finale is in the tonic B♭ major and it is closed in the normal way by a
tonic arpeggio / tonic triad in the strings.  
In the manuscript / the usual Boosey & Hawkes / Dover engraving the
first-violin closing gesture of the Allegro molto, IV, is

F5 – D5 – B♭4

the F – D – B♭ arpeggio of the final B♭-major tutti that is held
under the last fermata.  The attack that is heard last, and the lowest
of the three attacks of the closing gesture, is the tonic

B♭

i.e. the B♭ that anchors the final B♭–D–F B♭-major chord, written in
the score as the B♭ in the 3rd space / B♭4 in sounding pitch,
conventionally quoted as B♭3 in scientific pitch nomenclature.  It is
the root of the final B♭-major triad and the lowest pitch the first
violin actually sounds in the last three notes of the movement.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The finale is written in B♭ major and the first-violin line is
brought to a close with the little tonic arpeggio that introduces the
final tutti. In the Breitkopf/ Eulenburg – and in the IMSLP – engraving
of the IV. Allegro vivace the first violins are written in the last two
bars

   b♭′ – g′ – e♭′

on the way down to the final tonic sonority, the e♭′ being the written
e♭ above the stave, i.e. concert e♭4 – e♭5 written – the lowest of the
three pitches that the desk actually plays before the final fermata.
In the more usual “B♭–F–D’’ reading of the same descending B♭-major
arpeggio the three written pitches are b♭′–f′–d′ and the lowest
sounding pitch of the little closing figure is the d′ of the triad,
the written-sound equivalent of the e♭′ that is quoted in most modern
performing editions. That is the E♭/D that lies underneath the final
B♭–G–E♭–B♭ close of the first-violin line, the E♭ being the lowest
concert pitch that the first desk actually sounds at the very end of
Op.4.

5.text:
The finale is in B flat major and the close is a normal perfect-authentic
B flat-major close.  In the full score the first-desk is brought down to
the tonic triad in the last coda and the three distinct sounding pitches
that the part has just before the final fermata are the three members of
the tonic triad

     B♭ – D – F

written in the first-violin stave as a descending B flat-major arpeggio
F5 – D5 – B♭4 in the usual performing edition.  The bottom pitch of the
three is the tonic

     B♭

the B♭ that is the root of the final B♭–D–F chord, in the part the
B♭ that sits on the third line / just below the top of the stave, i.e.
about B♭4 in the third octave, the last note heard in the first-violin
line.  In the usual reading of the last three sounding pitches as
F – D – B♭ the last – and therefore the lowest – sounding pitch is the
final tonic B♭, the F being the lowest of the first two members of the
arpeggio.

8.text:
In the full-score edition that Dvořák finally allowed to be printed the
coda of the I. Allegro con fuoco is written out in the usual
nineteenth-century way.

The first violins come back to the closing B♭-major tutti with the
little cadential turn that Dvořák uses all through the finale

```
   b♭′  a′  g′
```

i.e. in the printed part

*   b♭4 – the top note of the closing turn,
*   a4 – the natural leading-note appoggiatura to the tonic,
*   g4 – the neighbour which is left sounding in the first-violin
    line just before the whole orchestra is brought in on the final
    B♭–D–F tutti.

In that little three-note gesture the third note of the turn is the
lowest, the G♮ of the B♭-major scale, normally printed as g′/g″
according to the edition.  It is the g′ that the first-violin line
actually leaves the stage on, the tutti then settling on the tonic
triad B♭–D–F, the lowest violin pitch of the final B♭-major chord
being the tonic B♭ itself. ∎

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The fourth movement closes in B♭ major on a normal
B♭–major tutti.  In the very last coda the first–violin line is written
as the little closing tag that Dvořák puts on the tune

    B♭‘–A‘–G‘

the three–note descending figure which is held under the final fermata
on the tonic.  In the sounding register that is the B♭ in the third
octave, the A in the third octave and the G in the third octave.  It
is the G which is the lowest of the three written pitches of the tag,
the G which sits a 2nd below the tonic B♭ that the violins finish on.
It is the F which is the lowest triad–tone of the final B♭-major
sonority that the first violins are actually sustaining at the
fermata, i.e. the F–above-middle-C / F4 of the B♭–major triad B♭–D–F,
F being the bottom note of the triad in the first-violin register.

1.text:
In the B flat major key of the work the fourth movement closes with a
fortissimo perfect authentic cadence on the tonic.  In the copy of the
part the coda is written out as the tonic triad

    B♭ – D – F

in the first violin.  In the form in which it is normally printed the
triad is realised as the little upward arpeggiation

       D4 – F4 – B♭4

that is the three successive pitches with which the desk actually
dies away, the three notes of the closing B♭ major triad.  In pitch-
class terms the bottom member of the final triad is the tonic B♭,
the bottom note of the three-note figure that is written out in the
part being the third of the triad, D, the D in the second space of the
first-violin staff, D4, rising to F4 and finally to the tonic B♭4.  That
is the familiar B♭-major final sonority of Op.4, the B♭ being the
lowest member of the triad and the D the lowest note of the
three-note arpeggiation as written.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think the lowest of the three closing first-violin notes is E natural. In the Allegro vivace finale the last bars are a firm B♭-major cadence and the first violins come in on the top of the tonic triad and then drop off for the final tag. In the printed B.46 score the closing violin figure is written as a little descending turn B♭–G–E, with the E being the last sounding pitch of the section and clearly the lowest of the three notes that the desk holds in the final bar. That E sits under the G that precedes it and the B♭ that starts the figure, which matches the usual B♭-major colour of the ending even though the line is a little lower than one might expect from the tutti.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: E. In the closing bars of the fourth movement, Allegro con fuoco, the first violins take the final tag over the tonic B♭ major cadence. The part is written in the last full measure and the spill-over into the final bar with a short three-pitch descending turn that leads into the final tutti. In the standard edition those three written pitches are B♭ – G – E, the G being the upper neighbor and the E being the lowest of the three articulated notes before the section is cut off by the final orchestral B♭ major chord. That E is the note that sits underneath the G and B♭ in the violin line and is the lowest pitch the first desk actually plays in that closing gesture.

15.text:
The Fourth Movement is in B flat major and the work is closed by a
fortissimo tonic tutti. In the 1865 B. 19/Op.4 score the first violins
close the coda with the tonic triad of the movement, the normal
cadential arpeggiation of B flat major

        F – D – B flat

in the penultimate bar and the final B flat fermata in the last bar.
In the usual up-beat notation the three successive first-violin
pitch classes which are written at the very end of the piece are

* B flat – D – F

of the tonic triad, written in the final bar as the descending
arpeggiation F5 – D5 – B flat4, the B flat being the fermata tonic
that the whole orchestra holds.

In pitch-class terms the lowest member of the closing triad is the
tonic B flat, the last sounding note of the violins being the final
fermata B flat, i.e.  the B flat that closes the F–D–B flat arpeggiation,
about B flat4 in the ordinary edition. That is the lowest of the three
notes B flat/D/F with which the first violin part is written up to the
final cadence.  The three-note figure is commonly quoted as the
ascending tonic arpeggio B flat–D–F, whose lowest pitch class is the
tonic B flat.
